questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Explain heterogeneous fields in one collection
questions.stem: In a field biologist's survey, one specimen record gains a wingspan field while every other record omits it; what does the document store permit that a column table cannot?

options.text: It stores the extra field only where present without touching other records
It copies the field to every record with a null default value
options.misconception: confuses document flexibility with column backfill

options.text: It creates a separate table to hold the extra field as a join
options.misconception: treats a document like a relational join

options.text: It rejects the insert because the collection schema is fixed
options.misconception: assumes tables and documents share schema rules

questions.explanation: A document shape allows heterogeneous fields per record, so one specimen can carry wingspan while others do not; a column table would need the column everywhere. The tempting idea that nulls are auto-filled mistakes document storage for relational defaults.
questions.hint: Think about which structure forces every row to share columns.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: State the write-side cost of maintaining an index
questions.stem: During a biologist's monthly plant census, adding an index on collection date speeds reads but what write-side cost does it introduce?

options.text: It doubles storage by copying the whole table into the index
options.misconception: confuses index size with full table duplication

options.text: Each insert or update must also modify the index structure
It removes the need to validate foreign keys on writes
It converts write operations into read-only lookups
options.misconception: reverses the role of an index

questions.explanation: An index is a separate structure updated on every write, so inserts and updates pay extra work; it is not free storage and does not change validation. The tempting shortcut assumes indexes only help reads.
questions.hint: Remember an index is maintained on every write.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Interpret query plan operators in order
questions.stem: A field crew's query plan prints Seq Scan, Hash Join, Sort; a reviewer claims the plan description 'reads data, joins, then sorts' is wrong because...

options.text: Seq Scan means the rows are already sorted before scanning
options.misconception: misreads a sequential scan as an ordered scan

options.text: Hash Join requires a sorted input to build its table
options.misconception: confuses hash join with merge join

options.text: The description is accurate: scan reads all rows, join builds hash, sort orders output
Sort happens before the join in the printed plan order
options.misconception: reverses operator order in the plan

questions.explanation: The plan's three words describe scan, join, and sort in execution order; a sequential scan reads all rows, so calling it reading data is right. The mistaken critique either misreads scan semantics or reverses plan order.
questions.hint: Read the plan operators left to right as executed.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish server-sent events from two-way channels
questions.stem: In a biologist's live species-count dashboard, the server pushes updates to browsers; explain why this is server-sent events and not a two-way channel.

answer.exemplar: Server-sent events use a single HTTP connection where only the server sends messages to the client; the client cannot push data back over that same stream, so any client-to-server message needs a separate request.

questions.explanation: SSE is unidirectional from server to client over one HTTP stream, unlike a socket that allows both sides to send. The tempting confusion treats any live push as full duplex.
questions.hint: One direction means server to client only.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Identify websocket close and reopen steps
questions.stem: A field tablet's websocket drops after a tunnel; which option correctly pairs stage one detect close with stage two perform handshake?

options.text: Stage one ignores close frames; stage two reuses the old socket
options.misconception: ignores close detection and socket lifecycle

options.text: Stage one waits for timeout; stage two sends a plain HTTP GET
options.misconception: mistakes reopen for a normal page request

options.text: Stage one treats any byte as close; stage two skips upgrade
options.misconception: misidentifies close frames and upgrade step

options.text: Stage one handles the close event; stage two sends an upgrade request with the handshake key

questions.explanation: A websocket close must be observed first, then reopening requires a new HTTP upgrade handshake with the protocol key. The tempting shortcut tries to reuse a dead socket or skip the upgrade.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism behind ordering guarantees
questions.stem: In a biologist's specimen pipeline, messages arrive out of order; what actually delivers an ordering guarantee across consumers?

options.text: A single partition or sequenced log assigns one total order
The network always preserves send order across brokers
Adding more consumers automatically sorts messages
Timestamps alone establish a global order

questions.explanation: Ordering comes from a single sequenced partition or log, not from the network or consumer count. The tempting assumption that timestamps or more consumers sort traffic ignores clock skew and concurrency.
questions.hint: Look for the one sequence owner.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Relate batching window to latency tradeoff
questions.stem: A field biologist batches sensor readings every five seconds; what latency does that window buy and what does it cost?

options.text: It increases latency to zero while cutting CPU
It removes all latency by sending once per window
It lowers per-message overhead but delays each reading up to five seconds
It makes every reading arrive exactly on the second

questions.explanation: Batching trades throughput for latency: fewer overheads but each item waits for the window. The tempting belief that batching removes latency ignores the wait time.
questions.hint: Window size is the max wait.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Define the baseline for a delta sync
questions.stem: A biologist's tablet syncs only changed specimens since last sync; an engineer says the baseline is the server's current clock; what is wrong?

options.text: The baseline is the number of connected devices
The baseline is always the full dataset size
The baseline is the network round trip time
options.misconception: uses transport metric as data baseline

options.text: The baseline must be the client's last known version or cursor

questions.explanation: A delta is measured from the client's last acknowledged version or cursor, not from a clock or device count. The tempting shortcut using server time ignores missed or reordered updates.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Explain tombstone retention duration
questions.stem: A deleted specimen marker (tombstone) stays in a biologist's sync log; how long must it be kept and why?

answer.exemplar: A tombstone must be kept at least until every replica that could still hold the old record has synced and observed the deletion, otherwise a stale replica can resurrect the deleted specimen.

questions.explanation: Tombstones persist until all replicas observe the deletion; removing them early lets an offline replica reintroduce the record. The tempting shortcut deletes them immediately to save space.
questions.hint: Keep until all replicas see it.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose empty delta from clock skew
questions.stem: A biologist's tablet clock is four minutes fast and the delta sync returns no changes even though specimens changed; what is the likely cause?

options.text: The server rejected the request due to authentication failure
options.misconception: blames auth instead of time comparison

options.text: The client's future timestamp makes the server think nothing changed after that time
The network dropped all packets silently
The database ran out of storage space

questions.explanation: A fast client clock can make the server's since-time comparison exclude recent changes, yielding an empty delta. The tempting guesses blame auth, network, or storage instead of time skew.
questions.hint: Compare the client timestamp to server time.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Recognize optional nested structures in documents
questions.stem: A biologist stores a specimen with an optional nested habitat object; a column table would need what extra handling for the same data?

options.text: It rejects nested data as invalid JSON
options.misconception: confuses storage model with JSON validation

options.text: It must create a separate table and join on every read
options.misconception: underestimates join cost but right idea

options.text: It can embed the nested object directly in the same record
It stores the nested object as a single string column

questions.explanation: Documents can embed nested objects in place, while relational tables split them into related rows and joins. The tempting simplification stores JSON as text or rejects nesting.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Estimate index maintenance on bulk writes
questions.stem: A biologist bulk-imports ten thousand specimen records with three indexes; why does the import take longer than the table size suggests?

options.text: Reads are blocked and queued
options.misconception: confuses read contention with write cost

options.text: The table is locked for the entire import
options.misconception: assumes a single lock explains all delay

options.text: Network compression slows the transfer
Indexes are rebuilt for each row, multiplying write work

questions.explanation: Each inserted row updates every index, so three indexes triple maintenance work beyond storing rows. The tempting explanations blame locks, network, or reads instead of index upkeep.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish scan types in a plan
questions.stem: A plan shows Index Scan instead of Seq Scan for a biologist's specimen lookup; a junior says this means the database reads fewer rows; is that always true?

options.text: Yes, index scan always reads exactly one row
options.misconception: assumes index scan is point lookup

options.text: No, it may still scan many index entries before fetching rows
No, index scan ignores the table entirely
Yes, index scan skips all nonmatching rows

questions.explanation: An index scan can traverse many entries and then fetch rows, so it is not guaranteed to read one row. The tempting overstatement treats any index use as a point lookup.
questions.hint: Index scans can be range scans.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Choose SSE for server push only
questions.stem: A biologist wants live counts pushed to a browser with no client uploads; why is SSE a fit?

answer.exemplar: SSE fits because it provides a simple server-to-client stream over HTTP, automatically reconnects, and avoids the overhead of a full duplex socket when the client never needs to send data.

questions.explanation: SSE is designed for server push with built-in reconnect and less complexity than a socket when no client messages are needed. The tempting alternative opens a duplex channel unnecessarily.
questions.hint: No client uploads means no socket needed.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Handle websocket close and reopen correctly
questions.stem: After a biologist's tablet loses wifi, the websocket closes; what should the client do next to resume updates?

options.text: Reuse the closed socket object immediately
options.misconception: ignores that closed sockets cannot be reused

options.text: Poll the REST endpoint forever instead
Create a new connection and complete the upgrade handshake
Send a close frame and wait for the server

questions.explanation: A closed websocket cannot be reused, so the client must open a new connection and repeat the upgrade handshake. The tempting workarounds reuse dead sockets or switch protocols entirely.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Recognize ordering requires a single owner
questions.stem: A biologist's event log claims global order; which setup actually provides it?

options.text: Multiple partitions with round-robin producers
Random broker assignment per message
Many consumers reading the same topic
A single partition consumed by one consumer

questions.explanation: Global order requires a single sequence owner like one partition; fanning out across partitions or consumers breaks it. The tempting scale-out patterns destroy the very guarantee.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Compute max latency from batch window
questions.stem: If a biologist's batch window is two seconds, what is the maximum added latency for a reading that arrives just after a batch sends?

options.text: Zero seconds because batching is instant
Exactly one second on average always
Up to two seconds until the next window closes
Four seconds due to double buffering

questions.explanation: A reading arriving right after a send waits for the full two-second window. The tempting answers claim instant delivery, fixed averages, or invented delays.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Use a version cursor for delta sync
questions.stem: A sync returns too many records because the biologist's tablet sends a timestamp instead of a version cursor; what is the flaw?

options.text: Timestamps always return fewer records
Version cursors are slower to compare
The server ignores all client input
Timestamps can collide or skew across devices

questions.explanation: Timestamps suffer from clock skew and collisions, so a version cursor is safer for deltas. The tempting preference for timestamps ignores time inconsistencies.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Avoid premature tombstone deletion
questions.stem: A biologist's sync log deletes tombstones after one day to save space; what risk does that create?

answer.exemplar: Deleting tombstones early can let an offline replica that has not synced the deletion resurrect the removed specimen, because it never sees the delete marker.

questions.explanation: Premature tombstone removal allows stale replicas to reintroduce deleted records. The tempting space-saving shortcut breaks eventual consistency.
questions.hint: Offline replicas still need the marker.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Fix clock skew in sync requests
questions.stem: A biologist's tablet clock is four minutes fast, causing empty deltas; which fix addresses the root cause?

options.text: Increase the batch size to ten thousand
Disable delta sync and always full sync
options.misconception: avoids rather than fixes the cause

options.text: Sync server time to the client before requesting deltas
Compress the payload to zero bytes

questions.explanation: Aligning client time with server time fixes the since-time comparison; scaling batches or disabling deltas only masks it. The tempting workarounds avoid the root cause.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Compare array storage in documents and tables
questions.stem: A biologist stores a specimen's tag list as an array field; how does a document handle this compared with a column table?

options.text: It splits tags across multiple records automatically
It requires one column per possible tag
It rejects arrays as non-scalar values
It stores the whole array in one field without a join table

questions.explanation: Documents embed arrays directly in the record, avoiding a separate join table. The tempting relational approaches add columns, reject arrays, or split records.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Recognize index cost on updates
questions.stem: When a biologist updates a specimen's location, which additional work occurs if an index exists on location?

options.text: The table is fully scanned to rebuild the index
The index is dropped and recreated from scratch
The index entry for the old value is removed and a new one inserted
No index work occurs on updates

questions.explanation: An update on an indexed field removes the old index entry and inserts a new one. The tempting extremes say the whole index rebuilds or that no work happens.
questions.hint: Update means delete plus insert in the index.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Read a plan's join type
questions.stem: A plan says Nested Loop Join for a biologist's specimen-to-habitat lookup; a reviewer claims it is always slower than hash join; what is missing?

options.text: Join type has no effect on performance
Hash join cannot use indexes at all
Nested loop always scans the whole table
Nested loop can be faster when the outer set is small and indexed

questions.explanation: Nested loops excel for small outer sets with index lookups, so declaring them always slower is wrong. The tempting absolutes ignore input size and index availability.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Handle SSE reconnect behavior
questions.stem: A biologist's dashboard loses connection; how does SSE recover without custom code?

answer.exemplar: The browser's EventSource automatically reconnects to the SSE endpoint and can resume using the last event id if the server supports it, so no manual retry loop is needed.

questions.explanation: EventSource handles reconnection automatically and may resume from the last event id. The tempting custom retry duplicates built-in behavior.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish close codes and reopen
questions.stem: A websocket closes with code 1006 (abnormal); what does that imply about the reopen process?

options.text: The server will reopen the socket automatically
The client must initiate a new connection and handshake
The socket can be resumed with the same id
No reopen is possible after 1006

questions.explanation: An abnormal close ends the connection, so reopening requires a new client-initiated connection and handshake. The tempting assumptions expect auto-reopen or permanent failure.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Explain sequence numbers in logs
questions.stem: A biologist's append-only log assigns sequence numbers; what guarantees order to consumers?

options.text: Consumers sort by arrival time
Brokers reorder messages on demand
The log's monotonic sequence numbers define order
Network FIFO guarantees order end to end

questions.explanation: Monotonic sequence numbers in the log define order; arrival time, broker reordering, or network FIFO are unreliable. The tempting alternatives ignore the assigned sequence.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Balance batch size and latency
questions.stem: A biologist can shrink the batch window to reduce latency; what tradeoff should be considered?

options.text: Smaller windows remove the need for ordering
Smaller windows eliminate all overhead
Smaller windows guarantee zero latency
Smaller windows raise per-message overhead and lower throughput

questions.explanation: Smaller windows reduce wait time but increase per-batch overhead and lower throughput. The tempting answers promise free gains or unrelated benefits.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Avoid full sync when delta possible
questions.stem: A biologist's app always full-syncs a large dataset; an engineer proposes delta sync but worries about missed deletes; how are deletes handled?

options.text: Deletes are ignored and never synced
Deletes require a full sync each time
Tombstones carry deletions in the delta stream
Deletes are inferred from missing records

questions.explanation: Tombstones propagate deletions through delta streams, so deltas can stay incremental. The tempting shortcuts ignore deletes or force full syncs.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Set tombstone retention by sync frequency
questions.stem: How long should a biologist's sync system keep tombstones if devices sync at least weekly?

answer.exemplar: Keep tombstones longer than the longest expected offline interval, such as two to three weeks, so every device that syncs weekly observes the deletion before the marker is removed.

questions.explanation: Retention must exceed the longest offline gap; weekly sync implies at least two weeks. The tempting short retention risks resurrection by offline devices.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Detect clock skew from empty deltas
questions.stem: A biologist sees an empty delta despite recent changes; which diagnosis best fits clock skew?

options.text: The client clock is behind the server and excludes nothing
The table is empty on the server
The network is too slow to return rows
The client clock is ahead, so the since-time is in the future

questions.explanation: A fast client clock makes the since-time future, excluding changes. The tempting alternatives reverse skew or blame network or empty data.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Identify schema evolution ease
questions.stem: A biologist adds a new field to specimen records over time; why is this easier in a document store?

options.text: The field is added to every record automatically
All records must be rewritten immediately
No migration is needed for old records to coexist
Schema changes are forbidden in documents

questions.explanation: Documents allow new fields without migrating old records, which can remain as-is. The tempting misconceptions demand immediate rewrites or backfills.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Weigh index count against write throughput
questions.stem: A biologist's write throughput drops after adding five indexes; what is the primary cause?

options.text: The table has too few rows
Reads are blocked by write locks
Network bandwidth is exhausted
Each write updates five index structures

questions.explanation: Five indexes mean five extra structures updated per write, reducing throughput. The tempting explanations blame locks, network, or row count instead of index maintenance.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Spot a sort node in a plan
questions.stem: A plan for a biologist's specimen list shows Sort with high cost; what does that indicate?

options.text: The sort is free because data is already ordered
Sort means the query returns no rows
The database must reorder a large result set
Sort eliminates duplicate rows automatically

questions.explanation: A costly sort means the database is ordering a large result set, which takes CPU and memory. The tempting shortcuts assume free ordering, no rows, or distinct behavior.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Reject SSE when client must send data
questions.stem: A biologist's app needs to send commands from browser to server frequently; why is SSE alone insufficient?

answer.exemplar: SSE only carries server-to-client messages, so frequent client commands require separate HTTP requests or a bidirectional socket; relying on SSE alone would leave client input without a channel.

questions.explanation: SSE is unidirectional, so client commands need another channel. The tempting assumption that SSE covers both directions leaves input unsupported.
questions.hint: SSE is server to client only.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Use heartbeat to detect stale sockets
questions.stem: A biologist's websocket appears open but no data flows; what should happen before reopen?

options.text: Wait indefinitely for data to resume
Switch to polling permanently
Close the browser tab and reopen it
Send a ping and reopen only if no pong returns

questions.explanation: A heartbeat ping detects stale sockets before reopening, avoiding unnecessary reconnects. The tempting extremes wait forever, disrupt users, or abandon sockets.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Explain why partitions break global order
questions.stem: A biologist uses multiple partitions for throughput; why does global order disappear?

options.text: Consumers reorder messages randomly
Partitions sort messages alphabetically
Each partition has its own independent sequence
The network drops ordering only on Tuesdays

questions.explanation: Each partition maintains its own sequence, so no global order exists across partitions. The tempting explanations blame consumers or invent conditions.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Estimate throughput gain from batching
questions.stem: A biologist batches ten readings per window; what is the main throughput benefit?

options.text: Storage size becomes zero
Each reading arrives ten times faster
Latency drops to zero for all readings
Fewer round trips and less per-message overhead

questions.explanation: Batching improves throughput by reducing round trips and per-message overhead, not by making each item faster. The tempting claims promise zero latency or storage.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Handle gaps in delta cursors
questions.stem: A biologist's delta cursor jumps by ten; what does that imply about the sync?

options.text: The cursor is working perfectly
Ten records were duplicated
Ten records were skipped and may be missing
The server has no data

questions.explanation: A cursor jump indicates skipped records that may be missing and need reconciliation. The tempting interpretations claim duplicates, perfection, or empty data.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Avoid deleting tombstones early
questions.stem: Why is deleting a tombstone immediately after marking a specimen deleted dangerous?

answer.exemplar: Immediate deletion removes the only evidence of the delete, so any replica that has not synced can reintroduce the specimen, breaking eventual consistency.

questions.explanation: Tombstones must outlive the slowest replica's sync interval. The tempting space-saving deletion risks resurrection of deleted records.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Use server time for since parameter
questions.stem: How should a biologist's sync request determine the since-time to avoid clock skew?

options.text: Use the client's local clock directly
Always use zero to fetch everything
Use the network latency as the since value
Use the server's last sync timestamp returned previously

questions.explanation: Using the server's previously returned sync timestamp avoids client clock skew. The tempting choices reuse local time, latency, or full syncs.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Explain polymorphic records in one collection
questions.stem: A biologist stores bird and insect specimens in one collection with different fields; why is this natural for documents?

options.text: Documents enforce one schema for all records
Documents split records into separate tables automatically
Documents allow each record its own field set
Documents require all fields to be null first

questions.explanation: Documents permit each record to have its own fields, supporting polymorphic specimens in one collection. The tempting misconceptions enforce uniformity or backfill nulls.
questions.hint: Each record defines its own shape.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Compare write cost with and without indexes
questions.stem: A biologist considers removing an index to speed writes; what is the tradeoff?

options.text: Storage becomes infinite
Writes slow down further
Reads become instant
Writes speed up but reads on that field slow down

questions.explanation: Removing an index reduces write maintenance but removes read acceleration on that field. The tempting answers reverse effects or overstate gains.
questions.hint: Trade write speed for read speed.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Interpret filter predicate in a plan
questions.stem: A plan's Filter node removes rows after a scan; a junior says it is useless because the scan already read them; what is the flaw?

options.text: Filter adds rows to the result
Filter rewrites the table permanently
Filter reduces rows before later operators and output
Filter only works on indexes

questions.explanation: Filter reduces the row set for subsequent operators and final output, even though the scan read them. The tempting misconceptions treat filter as useless, destructive, or index-only.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Use SSE for live notifications
questions.stem: Why is SSE a good fit for a biologist's live alert feed that only the server generates?

answer.exemplar: SSE is ideal because the server alone generates alerts, the browser handles reconnection automatically, and no client-to-server channel is required for a one-way notification feed.

questions.explanation: One-way server-generated alerts match SSE's strengths and avoid duplex complexity. The tempting alternative opens an unnecessary socket.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Handle reopen backoff
questions.stem: A biologist's websocket repeatedly fails to reopen; what strategy prevents hammering the server?

options.text: Retry immediately in a tight loop
Open ten sockets at once
Never retry after first failure
Use exponential backoff between reopen attempts

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff spaces reopen attempts and reduces server load. The tempting extremes retry instantly, give up, or multiply connections.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Use a single writer for order
questions.stem: A biologist needs strict order across all specimen events; what configuration achieves it?

options.text: Random partition selection per event
Many partitions with many producers
One partition with one producer
Consumers reordering by type

questions.explanation: A single partition and producer preserve a total order; scaling out partitions or producers breaks it. The tempting scale-out patterns destroy ordering.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Choose window by latency budget
questions.stem: A biologist needs p99 latency under one second; how should the batch window be set?

options.text: Set the window to exactly one second
Set the window to five seconds for throughput
Disable batching entirely always
Set the window well below one second

questions.explanation: The window must stay below the latency budget with margin; five seconds violates it and disabling batching is unnecessary. The tempting extremes either break the budget or overcorrect.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Recover from stale cursor
questions.stem: A biologist's device has a cursor older than server retention; what should the server do?

options.text: Return an empty delta and pretend success
Return an error forcing a full resync
Return random records
Delete the client's data

questions.explanation: When the cursor is too old, the server should signal the client to full resync rather than return incomplete or false data. The tempting shortcuts hide gaps or destroy data.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Compaction and tombstone cleanup
questions.stem: When can a biologist's sync store safely compact tombstones?

answer.exemplar: Compaction is safe only after confirming all replicas have synced past the tombstone's deletion point, ensuring no offline device can resurrect the record.

questions.explanation: Compaction requires all replicas to have observed the deletion. The tempting early compaction risks resurrection by lagging devices.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Explain empty delta from future since-time
questions.stem: A biologist's delta is empty despite changes; which root cause matches a fast client clock?

options.text: The server has no changes at all
The client's since-time is in the past and returns too much
The client's since-time is in the future relative to server
The network compressed the response to empty

questions.explanation: A fast client clock makes the since-time future, so the server returns no changes. The tempting alternatives reverse skew or blame data or network.

questions.topic: What a document shape permits that a table of columns cannot
questions.learningObjective: Recognize lack of join requirement
questions.stem: A biologist's specimen and its habitat details live in one document; what does this avoid?

options.text: Concurrency control entirely
All validation of input data
The need for any indexes
A join between separate tables on every read

questions.explanation: Embedding avoids joins on every read; it does not remove validation, indexing, or concurrency concerns. The tempting overstatements confuse embedding with unrelated features.

questions.topic: The write cost an index adds
questions.learningObjective: Index cost on deletes
questions.stem: When a biologist deletes a specimen, what index-related work occurs?

options.text: All indexes are rebuilt from scratch
The matching index entry is removed
No index work occurs on delete
The table is fully scanned regardless

questions.explanation: Deleting a row removes its index entries; it does not rebuild all indexes or scan the table. The tempting extremes overstate or ignore index maintenance.

questions.topic: Reading the three words a plan uses to describe its work
questions.learningObjective: Read an aggregate node
questions.stem: A plan shows Aggregate for a biologist's species count; a junior says it only counts rows; what else can it do?

options.text: It deletes duplicate rows
It only counts and cannot group
It can group, sum, average, and compute min or max
It sorts the output automatically

questions.explanation: Aggregate nodes can group and compute sums, averages, min, and max, not just count. The tempting understatements limit aggregates to counting or confuse them with distinct or sort.

questions.topic: A server-sent event and the one direction it allows
questions.learningObjective: Keep SSE connection alive
questions.stem: How does a biologist's SSE endpoint prevent proxies from closing an idle stream?

answer.exemplar: It sends periodic comment lines or heartbeat events over the stream, keeping the connection active so proxies and browsers do not time it out.

questions.explanation: Periodic heartbeats keep idle SSE streams alive against proxy timeouts. The tempting assumption that the connection stays open forever ignores proxy idle limits.

questions.topic: A socket that closes and the handshake that reopens it
questions.learningObjective: Handle reopen authentication
questions.stem: When a biologist's websocket reopens after a drop, what must be repeated to keep data flowing?

options.text: Nothing; the old session persists forever
The entire database migration
Only the close frame
The authentication and subscription steps

questions.explanation: Reopening requires repeating authentication and subscriptions because the old session is gone. The tempting shortcuts assume persistence or minimal frames.

questions.topic: What actually delivers an ordering guarantee
questions.learningObjective: Use sequence numbers for replay
questions.stem: A biologist replays specimen events; what ensures they process in original order?

options.text: Processing by arrival time at the consumer
Processing by event size
Processing by the log's sequence number
Processing by random selection

questions.explanation: Replay must follow the log's sequence numbers, not arrival time or size. The tempting alternatives cannot reconstruct original order.

questions.topic: A batching window and the latency it buys with
questions.learningObjective: Explain adaptive batching
questions.stem: A biologist's system shrinks the batch window under low load; why?

options.text: To double storage usage
To increase latency for all readings
To disable ordering guarantees
To reduce latency when throughput demand is low

questions.explanation: Adaptive batching shrinks windows under low load to reduce latency while throughput demand is low. The tempting alternatives reverse goals or invoke unrelated effects.

questions.topic: A delta sync and the baseline it is measured from
questions.learningObjective: Measure delta from last acknowledged version
questions.stem: A biologist's delta baseline uses the last sent version instead of last acknowledged; what can go wrong?

options.text: The server deletes all data
The sync becomes faster always
Unacknowledged changes may be skipped on failure
No difference exists between sent and acknowledged

questions.explanation: Using sent rather than acknowledged versions can skip changes if delivery fails. The tempting assumptions ignore network failures.

questions.topic: How long a tombstone has to be kept
questions.learningObjective: Set retention based on offline devices
questions.stem: A biologist has devices offline for up to a month; how long should tombstones remain?

answer.exemplar: Tombstones should remain for at least a month plus safety margin, covering the longest offline device so it can observe deletions before compaction.

questions.explanation: Retention must exceed the longest offline interval. The tempting shorter retention risks resurrection by offline devices.

questions.topic: A client clock four minutes fast and an empty delta set
questions.learningObjective: Resolve empty delta from clock skew
questions.stem: A biologist's empty delta persists after time sync; what should be checked next?

options.text: Whether the user changed passwords
Whether the network is unplugged
Whether the database is deleted
Whether the cursor was reset to zero

questions.explanation: After fixing clock skew, a stuck cursor may still cause empty deltas, so check the cursor state. The tempting alternatives are unrelated or extreme.
